name: Octinoxate
lead: Octinoxate (octyl methoxycinnamate, ethylhexyl methoxycinnamate, OMC) is an organic UVB filter used in sunscreens, lip balms and cosmetics with SPF claims [1][2]. It absorbs UVB with a peak near 310 nm and is typically combined with other filters [2].

It has drawn regulatory and scientific attention for endocrine activity seen in laboratory and animal studies, for systemic absorption in humans, and for its use being restricted in places such as Hawaii and Palau on environmental grounds [1][2]. The European Commission's Scientific Committee on Consumer Safety (SCCS) published an opinion in June 2025 concluding it is safe at up to 10% in cosmetics, according to both encyclopedia sources [1][2].
infobox: Octyl methoxycinnamate, ethylhexyl methoxycinnamate, Eusolex 2292, Uvinul MC80

paras: Octinoxate is described as the most common UVB-absorbing active ingredient in sunscreens and is often combined with oxybenzone and titanium dioxide [2]. It appears on US labels for lip balms and SPF products, often alongside avobenzone, octisalate and octocrylene [3].

It is a colourless to pale-yellow oily ester of methoxycinnamic acid and 2-ethylhexanol that is insoluble in water [1][2]. Under sunlight it isomerises from the E to the Z form, reducing UV absorption, which is why stabilisers are used [1][2].

A 2001 study of UV screens reported estrogenic activity in cultured cells and in rat experiments for several filters [4]. A 2004 review updated findings on endocrine activity and developmental toxicity of cosmetic UV filters [5]. In a human study, researchers measured systemic absorption of octinoxate, benzophenone-3 and 4-methylbenzylidene camphor after whole-body application alongside reproductive hormone levels [6], and a later study measured filters in plasma and urine after repeated application [7]. A 2020 JAMA trial found octinoxate and other ingredients in plasma after sunscreen use [8]. A 2017 review discussed possible neurotoxic effects of sunscreen ingredients, mainly from laboratory work [9].

Wikipedia lists a 2009 experimental study in which octinoxate reduced postoperative peritoneal adhesions, and notes lab studies reporting genotoxic effects of its isomers [2]; Grokipedia states that causal links to human health outcomes lack large-scale clinical data [1].

Reviews have examined effects of octinoxate and other sunscreen ingredients on coral reefs [10]. Hawaii and Palau have restricted it, and Wikipedia reports it was placed on the EU's 2019 priority list of potential endocrine disruptors before the June 2025 SCCS opinion found it safe at up to 10% [2].

Human research is mainly pharmacokinetic. A phase 1 programme enrolled 72 participants and measured absorption of six sunscreen ingredients including octinoxate [11][8], and the 2004 study measured absorption and reproductive hormones [6]. A 1,000-person European photopatch study examined photoallergy to sunscreen ingredients generally [12]. No trial found tests octinoxate alone for appearance outcomes.

timeline.event: Study of UV screens reports estrogenic activity in cell and rat assays [4].
Human study measures absorption of octinoxate and other filters and reproductive hormones [6].

JAMA trial reports octinoxate in plasma after sunscreen use; Palau restriction takes effect [8][2].

card.summary: The common organic UVB filter in sunscreens and lip balms, absorbed into the blood and flagged for endocrine activity in lab work, yet judged safe at 10% by the EU's SCCS in 2025.
card.note: Restricted in Hawaii and Palau on reef grounds.

quick.overview:
Octinoxate is a chemical sunscreen filter that absorbs UVB, the burning part of sunlight. It is common in sunscreens, SPF lip balms and cosmetics.

It has been debated because lab studies reported hormone-like activity and trials show it enters the bloodstream. The EU's SCCS concluded in 2025 that it is safe up to 10%.
quick.mechanism: It absorbs UVB radiation (about 290-320 nm) and dissipates the energy as heat. Sunlight can convert it to a form that absorbs less, so it is usually stabilised with other filters [1][2].
quick.risks: Reported concerns are endocrine activity in cell and animal studies, systemic absorption, and coral reef effects; human clinical harm has not been shown in the studies listed. Hawaii and Palau restrict it. Allowed levels: 7.5% US, 10% EU.
